::: {.hero-lede}
# Rodents, land use, pathogen transmission and spillover

I study how people reshape the landscapes they live in, how small mammals respond, and what effects that has on the viruses they carry. Much of this work is on Lassa fever in West Africa.
:::

```{=html}
<ul class="gradient-key">
  <li style="--band: var(--hab-forest)">
    <strong>Closed forest</strong>
    <span>Forest specialists, with little direct contact with people. Rodent sampling here is rare.</span>
  </li>
  <li style="--band: var(--hab-farm)">
    <strong>Forest edge and bush</strong>
    <span>Regrowth and fallow at the human margin. Small-mammal diversity is expected to peak here.</span>
  </li>
  <li style="--band: var(--hab-village)">
    <strong>Agricultural</strong>
    <span>Crops and fallow. Wild and commensal species meet where crops add food.</span>
  </li>
  <li style="--band: var(--hab-dwelling)">
    <strong>Rural dwellings</strong>
    <span>Villages and their gardens, where crop pests peak and spillover is thought to occur.</span>
  </li>
  <li style="--band: var(--hab-periurban)">
    <strong>Peri-urban dwellings</strong>
    <span>Invasive commensals may offer new hosts for zoonotic pathogens. Poor infrastructure may increase contact between rodents and people.</span>
  </li>
  <li style="--band: var(--hab-town)">
    <strong>Urbanised dwellings</strong>
    <span>Few rodent-borne zoonoses are reported from dense cities. Sanitation and human behaviour may limit spillover.</span>
  </li>
</ul>
<p class="hero-credit">Original illustration, modified with Gemini Flash 3.8 and Claude Opus 5.5.</p>
```
